2749.title: [Bug]: `MeanAverageRecall` counts crowd targets as misses, so mAR is lower than pycocotools on COCO data
2749.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I have searched the issues and discussions and found no similar bug report.

### Bug

`sv.metrics.MeanAverageRecall` counts crowd targets (`targets.data["iscrowd"] == 1`) as objects the model missed. In COCO evaluation a crowd region is an ignore region: it is never a miss, and a prediction on it is not a hit. `DetectionDataset.from_coco` stores `iscrowd` by default (`use_iscrowd=True`) and `MeanAveragePrecision` honours it, so on any COCO dataset with crowd annotations, mAR from supervision is lower than `pycocotools` AR. The same holds for the `data["ignore"]` flag that `MeanAveragePrecision` also reads.

In `mean_average_recall.py` the ignore mask passed to the confusion matrix is always zeros, and crowd targets stay in the denominator of every class's recall.

One normal target, one crowd target and one perfect prediction:

| | AR@100 | ARs |
|---|---|---|
| pycocotools 2.0.11 | 1.0 | -1 (no non-ignored small target) |
| sv `develop` | 0.5 | 0.0 |

On a seeded harness with 0–3 crowd targets per image (100 trials, boxes), mAR differs from `pycocotools` in 77 of 100 trials on `develop`.

### Environment

- supervision `develop` @ 927dfeb05 (0.31.0)
- macOS arm64, Python 3.12.13, NumPy 2.3.1, pycocotools 2.0.11

### Minimal Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import supervision as sv
from supervision.metrics import MeanAverageRecall

targets = sv.Detections(
    xyxy=np.array([[0, 0, 50, 50], [100, 0, 200, 100]], dtype=np.float32),
    class_id=np.array([0, 0]),
    data={"iscrowd": np.array([0, 1])},
)
predictions = sv.Detections(
    xyxy=np.array([[0, 0, 50, 50]], dtype=np.float32),
    class_id=np.array([0]),
    confidence=np.array([0.9]),
)
print(MeanAverageRecall().update(predictions, targets).compute().mAR_at_100)
# 0.5   (pycocotools AR@100: 1.0)
```

2751.title: [Bug]: oriented-box IoU exactly on 0.55/0.6/0.8/0.85 misses that threshold in MeanAverageRecall, Precision, Recall and F1Score
2751.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I have searched the issues and discussions and found no similar bug report.

### Bug

With `metric_target=MetricTarget.ORIENTED_BOUNDING_BOXES`, a prediction whose IoU is exactly 0.55, 0.6, 0.8 or 0.85 is counted as a miss at that threshold by `MeanAverageRecall`, `Precision`, `Recall` and `F1Score`. The same geometry as `BOXES` counts as a match, and so does `MeanAveragePrecision`.

The thresholds are `np.linspace(0.5, 0.95, 10, dtype=np.float32)` (`mean_average_recall.py` and `_confusion_matrix_metric.py`). In float32, 0.55, 0.6, 0.8 and 0.85 round up, so 0.6 becomes 0.6000000238. `box_iou_batch` and `mask_iou_batch` return float32, so an exact 0.6 IoU equals the float32 threshold. `oriented_box_iou_batch` returns float64, so the same 0.6 falls just below it. #2638 fixed this kind of float32/float64 mismatch for `MeanAveragePrecision` and listed these four metrics as out of scope.

### Environment

- supervision `develop` @ 927dfeb05 (0.31.0)
- macOS arm64, Python 3.12.13, NumPy 2.3.1

### Minimal Reproducible Example

Target `[0, 0, 10, 10]`, prediction `[0, 1, 14, 11]`: overlap 90, union 150, IoU 0.6.

```python
import numpy as np
import supervision as sv
from supervision.config import ORIENTED_BOX_COORDINATES
from supervision.metrics import MetricTarget, Recall


def detections(xyxy, confidence=None):
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = xyxy
    return sv.Detections(
        xyxy=np.array([xyxy], dtype=np.float64),
        class_id=np.array([0]),
        confidence=None if confidence is None else np.array([confidence]),
        data={ORIENTED_BOX_COORDINATES: np.array([[[x0, y0], [x1, y0], [x1, y1], [x0, y1]]], dtype=np.float64)},
    )


predictions, targets = detections([0, 1, 14, 11], 0.9), detections([0, 0, 10, 10])
for target in (MetricTarget.BOXES, MetricTarget.ORIENTED_BOUNDING_BOXES):
    print(target, Recall(metric_target=target).update(predictions, targets).compute().recall_scores[:3])
# MetricTarget.BOXES                    [1. 1. 1.]
# MetricTarget.ORIENTED_BOUNDING_BOXES  [1. 1. 0.]   <- the 0.6 threshold misses
```

2689.title: [Bug]: MeanAverageRecall limits detections per image, pycocotools limits them per image and class
2689.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I have searched the issues and discussions and found no similar bug report.

### Bug

`MeanAverageRecall` applies the mAR@K limit to each image across all classes. pycocotools applies `maxDets` to each image *and category*: `COCOeval.evaluateImg(imgId, catId, aRng, maxDet)` only sees the detections of one category in one image and keeps the top `maxDet` of those. So with more than one class, `mAR@1`, `mAR@10` and `mAR@100` come out lower than the COCO AR values.

`MeanAveragePrecision` already uses the per-class limit and matches pycocotools on the same data. Only mAR differs.

`test_mar_at_k_limits_per_image_not_per_class` pins the current behavior and describes the per-class limit as the bug. From #1966 and #2136 I understood the goal was to match COCO, and the maintainer comment there asked to reopen if mAR still didn't match COCO, so I'm raising it here before sending a PR.

**Expected:** mAR@K equal to pycocotools AR@K (`stats[6:9]`).

**Actual:** one image, two classes, two perfect predictions: supervision mAR@1 = 0.5, pycocotools AR@1 = 1.0. On a larger example (2 images, 3 classes, 180 targets and 180 jittered predictions per image), supervision gives mAR@1/10/100 = 0.0025 / 0.0286 / 0.2772, and pycocotools gives 0.0089 / 0.0861 / 0.4881. mAP@50:95 is 0.3912 in both.

### Environment

- Supervision: 0.31.0.dev0 (develop at 3bc0301)
- pycocotools: 2.0.11
- Python: 3.12
- OS: Windows 11

### Minimal Reproducible Example

```python
import contextlib, io
import numpy as np
import supervision as sv
from pycocotools.coco import COCO
from pycocotools.cocoeval import COCOeval
from supervision.metrics import MeanAverageRecall

xyxy = np.array([[0, 0, 50, 50], [100, 100, 150, 150]], dtype=float)
targets = sv.Detections(xyxy=xyxy, class_id=np.array([0, 1]))
predictions = sv.Detections(xyxy=xyxy, class_id=np.array([0, 1]), confidence=np.array([0.9, 0.8]))
print(MeanAverageRecall().update(predictions, targets).compute().mAR_at_1)  # 0.5

gt = COCO()
gt.dataset = {
    "images": [{"id": 0}],
    "categories": [{"id": 0}, {"id": 1}],
    "annotations": [
        {"id": i + 1, "image_id": 0, "category_id": i, "bbox": [x0, y0, x1 - x0, y1 - y0],
         "area": (x1 - x0) * (y1 - y0), "iscrowd": 0}
        for i, (x0, y0, x1, y1) in enumerate(xyxy)
    ],
}
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    gt.createIndex()
    dt = gt.loadRes([
        {"image_id": 0, "category_id": i, "bbox": [x0, y0, x1 - x0, y1 - y0], "score": s}
        for i, ((x0, y0, x1, y1), s) in enumerate(zip(xyxy, [0.9, 0.8]))
    ])
    E = COCOeval(gt, dt, "bbox")
    E.evaluate(); E.accumulate(); E.summarize()
print(E.stats[6])  # 1.0
```

1449.body:
### Search before asking

- [X] I have searched the Supervision [issues](https://github.com/roboflow/supervision/issues) and found no similar feature requests.


### Description

Next to the count of the objects in the zone, it would be useful to know how much of the zone area is occupied by the objects.

### Use case

e.g. for loading zones in warehouses

### Additional

Basically I've implemented it myself outside of the PolygonZone class. The core of what is needed is these two functions:

```python
def polygon_to_binary_mask(img,contour):
    """convert bounding polygon coord to binary mask"""
    # Create binary mask
    b_mask = np.zeros(img.shape[:2], np.uint8)

    #  Extract contour result
    #contour = c.masks.xy.pop()
    #  Changing the type
    contour = contour.astype(np.int32) #Note: This must be int32 and not unit8!!!
    #  Reshaping
    contour = contour.reshape(-1, 1, 2)


    # Draw contour onto mask
    mask = cv2.drawContours(b_mask, [contour], -1, (1, 1, 1), cv2.FILLED)
    return mask
```

#### strategy: 
1) make union of binary masks of detected objects (only the classes for consideration in zone)
2) make binary mask of the zone
3) do and of zone mask & object masks
4) sum the 1 pixels

```python
def calculate_overlap_area(zone_mask, masks,show_plot=True):
    """calculate how much % of the zone is occupied"""
    #create one mask from the object masks as the union
```

2845.title: [Feature]: Bit-packed dense mask IoU and NMM: identical results, ~20x less memory, 20-47x faster mask NMM
2845.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I have searched the issues and discussions and found no similar feature request.

### Feature Description

**What:** Compute dense-mask overlaps on bit-packed masks instead of float32 copies. Each mask is packed with `np.packbits` and viewed as `uint64` words. Pairwise intersections then come from `np.bitwise_count(a & b)`, and areas from `np.count_nonzero`. All counts are exact integers, so the existing IoU/IoS division code runs unchanged and gives the same result. No API change and no new dependency.

Two internal functions would change:

- [`_mask_iou_batch_split`](https://github.com/roboflow/supervision/blob/a87bb76905b631d995049bb5983ce99adfaebd1c/src/supervision/detection/utils/iou_and_nms.py#L988-L1053), which backs `mask_iou_batch`, `mask_non_max_suppression`, `mask_soft_non_max_suppression` and `Detections.with_nms` on dense masks.

- The matmul approach from #2323 casts both mask stacks to float32, so the working set is 32× the size of the packed bits.

### Search before asking

- [x] I have searched the issues and discussions and found no similar feature request.

### Feature Description

**What:** A small geometry-aware dispatch layer so detection ops use the geometry each detection actually carries (mask / OBB / box) instead of silently falling back to the axis-aligned `xyxy`.

**Why:** Several recent fixes are the same bug in different functions: code grabs `detections.xyxy` and forgets the real geometry lives in `data["xyxyxyxy"]` (OBB) or `mask`. Because `xyxy` is always present, the wrong answer is the silent default:
- `Detections.area` returned the AABB area, not the rotated body (#2306)
- `with_nms` / `with_nmm` dropped crossed OBBs via AABB IoU (#2303)
- `as_yolo` dropped OBB rotation on export (#2289)
- `roboflow/inference`: consensus IoU, and stitch / crop corner shifts (https://github.com/roboflow/inference/pull/2420, https://github.com/roboflow/inference/pull/2427, https://github.com/roboflow/inference/pull/2430)

Same root cause each time: `Detections` holds several geometries at once and `xyxy` is just a derived envelope, so every consumer re-implements "which geometry is the real one?" and forgetting it fails silently. The next geometry-aware function will hit it again.

**How:** Centralize the dispatch into a few batched helpers and route call sites through them instead of reaching for `xyxy`. No data-model change, keeps the vectorized design, backward compatible. Migration can be incremental, then deprecate the ad-hoc paths.

Proposed helpers (batched, no per-detection loops):
- `detection_iou(a, b)`: dispatches mask / OBB / box IoU
- `detection_area(det)`: mask sum / shoelace / box area
- `move_detections(det, offset)`: shifts `xyxy`, `mask`, OBB corners and keypoints together (what #2427 / #2430 each forgot)
- a `test_op_respects_geometry` contract test that fails when an op can't tell an OBB from its envelope

Rollout can be incremental and each step is independent / backward compatible: (1) consolidate the duplicated `move_detections` (pure dedup, no behavior change), (2) the read-only `detection_iou` / `detection_area` dispatch, (3) the contract test.

A first pass suggests more call sites in the same class worth investigating: `get_anchors_coordinates` (and therefore `LineZone` / `PolygonZone`) reads anchors off the envelope rather than the rotated body, `as_coco` and `as_pascal_voc` have no `is_obb` option and drop the rotation on export, `with_nmm` merges to the union envelope while keeping one input's `data["xyxyxyxy"]`, and `DetectionsSmoother` averages `xyxy` without smoothing the oriented corners.

    return box_area(det.xyxy)

2674.title: [Bug]: NumPy fallback draws thick rectangle borders inward instead of centering them on the edge
2674.body:
### Bug

**What's the bug?**

The NumPy fallback draws a stroked rectangle entirely *inside* the rectangle, while OpenCV centers the stroke on the rectangle's edges. Any box drawn with `thickness >= 2` therefore comes out thinner and smaller when `opencv-python` is not installed.

Since OpenCV is no longer a dependency, the fallback is what a plain `pip install supervision` uses, and `BoxAnnotator`'s default `thickness` is `2`, so this is the default path. `CropAnnotator` (default `border_thickness=2`), `PercentageBarAnnotator`'s border and `sv.draw_rectangle` (default `thickness=2`) reach the same call. The filled calls in `ColorAnnotator` and `LabelAnnotator` are unaffected.

**Expected behavior:** the fallback matches OpenCV, per the intent stated in #2433 and #2439.

**Actual behavior:** the border is drawn inward only. `thickness=1` and filled (`thickness=-1`) rectangles are unaffected.

| backend | painted px | painted bbox |
|---|---:|---|
| `opencv` | 596 | x 19-81, y 19-61 |
| `fallback` | 392 | x 20-80, y 20-60 |

For a `(3,3)` to `(11,8)` rectangle at `thickness=2`, OpenCV paints rows 2 to 9 and columns 2 to 12, its left band covering columns 2 to 4. The fallback paints rows 3 to 8 and columns 3 to 11, its left band covering only columns 3 and 4. The stroke is one pixel narrower and sits one pixel inside OpenCV's on every side.

**Cause:** `_rectangle` in `src/supervision/_cv2/_drawing.py` uses Pillow's `ImageDraw.rectangle(outline=1, width=thickness)`, and Pillow's `width=` only grows inward. OpenCV strokes each edge as a band centered on it and rounds the four joints with a filled disc, so the border spreads outside the rectangle as well as inside.

This was not caught because `test_fallback_line_draws_and_matches_opencv_extent` compares only the raster bounding box with `atol=1`, and the error at `thickness=2` is exactly 1 pixel per side.

### Feature Description

`sv.metrics` scores boxes, masks and oriented boxes, but as far as I can tell there is no metric for pose estimation yet. Evaluating a pose model on `sv.KeyPoints` currently means converting to COCO JSON and running `pycocotools`.

`pycocotools` remains the reference, and this would not try to replace it. The idea is to give supervision users the same numbers without the round trip:

- **No conversion.** `pycocotools` needs COCO JSON with image ids, annotation ids, categories and flattened `[x, y, v, ...]` arrays. With a metric on `sv.KeyPoints`, `metric.update(predictions, targets)` is enough.

- **Custom skeletons.** Non-human keypoints (animals, objects) only need a `sigmas=` argument instead of editing evaluator parameters.

It also adds an OKS helper and the COCO sigmas, kept private for now.

2476.title: match_detections(): expose the unified greedy matcher as a public cross-Detections primitive
2476.body:
## Search before asking

- [x] I have searched the supervision issues and found no similar feature request.

## Description

#2378 pointed out that `ConfusionMatrix` and `Recall`/`F1Score`/`MeanAverageRecall` were matching predictions to targets with different algorithms, and #2380 fixed it the same day by unifying everything onto one greedy matcher in `supervision/metrics/utils/matching.py` (`_greedy_match` + `_match_detection_batch_with_target_indices`). All five metric modules now delegate to it.

That matcher is exactly the primitive users keep needing outside metrics — "given two `Detections`, which instances correspond?" — but it's private and shaped for metric internals (pre-computed IoU matrix, class-index arrays, per-IoU-threshold correctness matrix, COCO-style scored/unscored rounds). There is no public API that takes two `Detections` and returns matched pairs. `box_iou_batch` is public, so today everyone hand-rolls the assignment step on top of it — with the same one-to-many/ordering bugs #2378 was about — or sidesteps geometry entirely with VLM calls (e.g. the planogram-compliance guide pairs an RF-DETR detector with two Gemini VQA calls, where the "which detection corresponds to which reference slot" half of the problem is a matching problem: https://blog.roboflow.com/planogram-compliance-detection/).

## Proposed API

```python
matched_pairs, unmatched_a, unmatched_b = sv.match_detections(
    detections_a,           # sv.Detections
    detections_b,           # sv.Detections
    iou_threshold=0.5,
    class_agnostic=False,
)
```

Returns index arrays, not new `Detections`, so it composes with existing slicing:

- `matched_pairs`: `np.ndarray` of shape `(M, 2)` — column 0 indexes into `detections_a`, column 1 into `detections_b`
- `unmatched_a`: `(len(detections_a) - M,)` indices into `detections_a`
- `unmatched_b`: `(len(detections_b) - M,)` indices into `detections_b`

`detections_a[unmatched_a]`, `detections_b[matched_pairs[:, 1]]`, etc. all just work.

### Semantics

| Case | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Assignment | one-to-one, greedy, highest-IoU-first — identical to `_greedy_match` from #2380 |
| IoU ties | stable order (`np.argsort(-iou, kind="stable")`), matching the internals |
| `class_agnostic=False` (default) | a pair additionally requires equal `class_id` — mirrors the `correct_class` mask in `_match_detection_batch_with_target_indices` |
| `class_agnostic=True` | IoU-only matching |
| IoU below `iou_threshold` | never paired, regardless of class |
| `detections_a` or `detections_b` empty | `matched_pairs.shape == (0, 2)`; every index of the other side is unmatched |
| `confidence` | ignored — the primitive is pure geometry+class; callers who want metric-style score ordering sort upstream |
| Symmetry | greedy-on-IoU makes `match_detections(a, b)` equal `match_detections(b, a)` with columns swapped (up to ordering among exactly-tied IoU pairs) |

2544.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I have searched the issues and discussions and found no similar bug report.

### Bug

**What's the bug?**

`DetectionDataset.from_pascal_voc` fails as soon as the dataset contains an image with no objects in it. A Pascal VOC XML file with a `<size>` block but no `<object>` entries is perfectly normal (it is how negative images are stored), but loading a directory that contains one raises an error and the whole dataset is lost.

The library's own exporter writes exactly this kind of file. `as_pascal_voc` on a dataset with an empty `Detections` produces an XML with no `<object>`, and `from_pascal_voc` then refuses to read it back, so the export and import are no longer a round trip.

This worked in 0.27.0 and earlier. It has been broken since 0.28.0 and is still broken on `develop`.

**Where it comes from**

In `src/supervision/dataset/formats/pascal_voc.py`, `detections_from_xml_obj` builds `class_id` like this:

```python
class_id = np.array(
    [extended_classes.index(class_name) for class_name in class_names]
)
```

- In 0.28.0 through 0.29.1 it indexes the class name array with `class_id` to fill in `class_name`, and NumPy rejects a float array as an index.
- On `develop` the dtype check added in #2410 catches it first and raises a `ValueError` instead.

The YOLO and COCO loaders both pass `dtype=int` when building `class_id`, so they load negative images fine. The VOC loader is the only one that does not.

An XML file with no objects should load as an empty `Detections` with an integer `class_id`, the same way an empty YOLO label file or a COCO image with no annotations does. Exporting a dataset with `as_pascal_voc` and loading it again with `from_pascal_voc` should give back the same dataset.

2756.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I have searched the issues and discussions and found no similar bug report.

### Bug

#2747 (with PR #2748) covers the `int()` truncation in the same function; this issue is about the remaining part, the +1 on xmax and ymax, which #2748 keeps.

`dataset/formats/pascal_voc.py` (line 72 in 0.30.9 and 0.31.0) adds 1 to all four coordinates before writing, citing #144 ("Pascal VOC coordinates are 1-indexed"). In the VOC devkit convention, pixel indices are 1-based and **inclusive**: a box covering 0-based pixels x0 .. x0+w-1 is written `xmin = x0 + 1`, `xmax = x0 + w`, so a box with `xmin=1, xmax=W` covers the whole image. Only xmin and ymin need the +1. Adding it to xmax and ymax makes every exported box one pixel wider and taller for readers that follow the devkit, such as Detectron2's `pascal_voc.py` loader, which subtracts 1 from xmin and ymin only.

supervision's reader subtracts 1 from all four coordinates (`xyxy_arr -= 1`), so a supervision -> supervision round trip looks exact, and the problem only appears when another tool reads the files. Reader and writer would need to change together.

This also affects #2747: with PR #2748, the 0-based box `[0, 0, 37, 29]` is written as `1 1 38 30`, but its devkit encoding is `1 1 37 29`. Integer boxes, which rounding does not change, are all one pixel too large on the right and bottom.

In our audit of COCO val2017 read with the devkit convention, 30% of the boxes exported by `as_pascal_voc` had IoU below 0.9 with their source box, most of them small objects; both the truncation and the +1 on xmax/ymax contribute, and #2748 removes only the first.

**Output of the example below:** `<xmin>11</xmin> <ymin>21</ymin> <xmax>41</xmax> <ymax>61</ymax>`. The devkit encoding of COCO box x=10, y=20, w=30, h=40 is 11, 21, 40, 60.

**Expected:** add 1 to xmin and ymin only when writing, and subtract 1 from xmin and ymin only when reading. Since #2748 is already changing this function, it may be simplest to fold the change into it. 781.title: [InferenceSlicer] - allow batch size inference
781.body:
### Description

Currently, [`sv.InferenceSlicer`](https://supervision.roboflow.com/detection/tools/inference_slicer/) processes each slice in a separate callback call - hindering inference with a batch size larger than 1. We can change this by:

- **Batching Slices:** Instead of submitting individual tasks for each slice, group slices into batches. `batch_size` can be a new parameter for the `InferenceSlicer` class.
- **Modifying the Callback:** Ensure the callback function can handle a batch of slices instead of a single slice.
